title: GPU vector search and corpus analytics
subtitle: Vectors that stay out of the database yet verifiably tied to it, searched and scored on the GPU

stats.label: recall at ten against exact search, the inverted-file floor asserted in continuous integration
relative tolerance between every kernel and its CPU reference
to rebuild the GPU files from four million rows, the cost a delta build avoids

lede: Embeddings are often too large and too hot for the relational database, and the moment they leave it there is no way to say which row a vector belongs to, or whether the index being searched is any good. I built vector storage leased to the GPU that stays verifiably tied to its relational source, with index-quality reporting so retrieval health is visible. See An index you can rebuild from its receipt and The database decides when an index goes stale. Under it is a CUDA engine written from Rust against the driver API for the newest NVIDIA architecture, with a CPU reference and equivalence tests for every kernel, and exact, inverted-file and lattice search.
quote: A GPU kernel that computes a statistic is a poor definition of that statistic.
evidence: Vector search and ANN indexes: exact, inverted-file and lattice search on the GPU, with a recall-at-ten floor of 0.85 against exact search asserted in continuous integration.
Data provenance for retrieval: every index build carries configuration, training-set and artifact hashes, and a rebuild from shuffled input gives byte-identical artifacts.
Database-driven index invalidation: a trigger marks every index over a shard stale the moment its journal advances, and the loader refuses a mismatched file with a reason.
Incremental rebuild design: delta builds byte-identical to the full build, chosen by shape with a full rebuild past 10% of the table or 100,000 pending rows, sparing a ~100 s full rebuild.
CUDA kernel development: kernels written from Rust against the driver API, each held to a CPU reference at a relative tolerance of 10⁻⁴.
Embedding analytics and cluster metrics: search and cluster health from the same read, through a NaN-filled side-band reduced to cohesion and inertia per cluster.
author: Corey James
